On September 2nd, 2026, we searched clinicaltrials.gov with the key words of ("conductive hydrogel" or "hydrogel electrode" or "hydrogel nerve interface" or "hydrogel bioelectronics") and (nerve regulation or "nerve stimulation" or "nerve recording" or "brain computer interface" or "peripheral nerve" or "spinal cord") [137]. As long as it is human intervention research, the evaluation is that the clinical transformation of the implanted or surgically placed conductive hydrogel interface or device has not been realized yet, which cannot be simply attributed to the fact that this field is not "new". In fact, there are several types of specific evidence missing and the project gap has not been filled.

First, we have not found any research that can simultaneously meet the following conditions in large animal models (pigs, sheep, dogs or non-human primates) on a clinical scale: implantation for at least six months, and complete recording of longitudinal signal-to-noise ratio or impedance trajectory, stimulus threshold changes, device displacement evaluation, and matched quantitative histopathology. Therefore, the long-term ECoG study on rabbits can only be regarded as evidence of non rodents, and should not be directly renamed as large animal validation.

Second, the stability at the material level has not yet been reliably translated into the verified service life of devices. Bench aging and immersion experiments can help us screen materials, but it is far from enough to prove that it can last for several years in a human body with quite complex mechanical and chemical environments.

Third, the consistency of manufacturing batches is still a bottleneck at present. Water content, crosslinking density, PEDOT:PSS doping state, CNT or MXene dispersion, ion composition, and the interface between hydrogel and electrode - any link fluctuation may cause obvious deviation in the electrical and mechanical properties of the batch.

Fourth, sterilization, packaging and storage cannot be treated as back-end details, but must be included in the overall verification of the final device. The effects of irradiation, ethylene oxide sterilization, dehydration and storage conditions on the mechanical properties, adhesion ability, chemical structure and electrochemical properties of hydrogels are closely related to the specific formula, and should be evaluated one by one by experiments. FDA guidelines also repeatedly emphasize that the sterilization process should be verified, and the impact of sterilization on device performance and biocompatibility should also be considered [143] (see Table 7).

Fifth, the long-term material safety must be evaluated for the final device, and cannot be concluded only by the label of body composition, antioxidant activity, short-term cell survival rate or "biocompatibility". Here, we make a distinction: direct evidence refers to the experimental data of the same final formula, the same anatomical target, the same exposure route, the same endpoint and duration; Indirect analogy refers to evidence from related materials, different cell types, different targets or device configurations; Hypothesis means that a benefit or risk has only been proposed at the conceptual level and has not been tested in the relevant chronic models. Table 8 maps these classifications to major chemical and biological risks. A complete risk management framework should integrate formula specific chemical characterization, extractable/extract analysis, toxicological risk assessment, and chronic tissue device endpoints under the framework of ISO 10993 and current FDA recommendations [144,145].

Sixth, the failure of the device is not necessarily due to the hydrogel itself. Most of the time, it is the hydrogel metal interconnection, package interface, tissue adhesion interface, wire transition, connector or package itself that have problems first. The dry-type double-sided tape mentioned in Fig. 8e may be useful as an assembly principle [130], but to use it in chronic nerve implants, targeted verification must be done for fatigue, sterilization, shelf life, extractable/extractable substances and interface reliability.

In a word, the clinical transformation should be done as the development of devices for specific targets, rather than the natural extension of the study of hydrogel materials. A feasible path should at least include: validation on clinical relevant anatomical scales, preset chronic electrophysiological and histological endpoints, manufacturing specifications and batch release standards, sterilization and aging validation, risk-based biological evaluation, and alignment with the applicable FDA or NMPA regulatory path as soon as possible.

Hydrogel bioelectronics is entering a key node to accelerate the transformation from laboratory innovation to clinical application. This review summarizes the main progress in this field, from which we can see that with the help of bionic design, multi-level structure engineering and interface functionalization, conductive hydrogels have gradually grown into a kind of "intelligent" interface materials that can dynamically adapt to nerve tissue, electrophysiological regulation and biological activity induction, which can take into account. Its core advantages have been gradually recognized in the chronic nerve regulation: the mechanical properties can be adjusted and matched, and the foreign body reaction after implantation can be reduced to a certain extent; The interface adhesion and anti swelling ability are online, and the stability of long-term electrical contact will not easily go wrong; There is a natural affinity with biological tissues, so there is a relatively favorable microenvironment for nerve repair and functional regulation. Together, these characteristics have pushed hydrogel bioelectronics to many application scenarios, such as peripheral nerve repair, brain computer interface, spinal cord injury regulation, and so on. In the face of traditional rigid electronic devices, hydrogel bioelectronics also shows some unique confidence.

In short, there are still many systemic challenges to move from laboratory to clinical application. The long-term stability and controllable degradation of implants, the maintenance of high fidelity signals in complex physiological environments, and the landing of wireless and miniaturized closed-loop systems are the most striking. From experimental prototypes to reliable medical devices, standardized and large-scale manufacturing processes and clear clinical transformation paths are all thresholds that must be crossed. Materials science, flexible electronics, neural engineering and clinical medicine need to be deeply integrated together. In the future, more efforts should be made on the robust hydrogel network, mixed ionic-electronic transport architecture, standardized preparation process, and systematic transformation evaluation framework. Only when these problems are solved one by one can hydrogel bioelectronics really take a step forward from the level of proof of concept.

The future development will probably focus more and more on two directions: one is to improve the intelligence of the material itself, and the other is to seek breakthroughs in system integration. If the intelligent hydrogel that can respond to multiple bio electro mechanical signals is integrated with sensing, feedback and executive functions, the adaptive and personalized neural regulation system is expected to become a reality. Once the challenges of long-term stability, wireless power supply, and large-scale manufacturing are successfully addressed, this technology has completed a substantial leap from cutting-edge concepts to clinical therapy. Nervous system diseases such as Parkinson's disease and chronic pain can probably wait for a new generation of precise, minimally invasive and lasting treatment options.

Accordingly, the translational endpoint proposed in this review is not an immediate jump from an optimized hydrogel to large-animal implantation. It is a NAM-enabled sequence in which neural organoids screen material formulations and network function; nerve-on-chip/MPS and targeted toxicity assays resolve interface injury; degradation and accelerated-ageing models identify long-term chemical, mechanical, and electrical failure; and computational models select device geometry, stimulation limits, and the focused questions to be tested in animals. Used as fit-for-purpose decision gates, these approaches can make chronic in vivo studies smaller, more targeted, and more informative while preserving animal confirmation for surgery, systemic biology, and long-duration performance [11,12,[131], [132], [133], [134], [135], [136]].

tables.caption: Comparative analysis of major conductive-hydrogel design paradigms for chronic neural interfaces.
rows: Design paradigm
Conductivity and mechanical profile
Chronic stability and cytocompatibility
Processability, cost, and representative evidence
Carbon-nanomaterial composite hydrogels (CNT, graphene/rGO)
Electronic percolation can provide high conductivity and, with good filler-matrix coupling, mechanical reinforcement.

Performance depends on dispersion and preservation of percolation during hydration and cyclic deformation. Medium-term neural studies can show favorable tissue responses, but long-term redistribution, release, and biological fate remain incompletely resolved.
Scale-up is sensitive to nanomaterial dispersion, aggregation, and surface functionalization. Device-level cost is rarely quantified [22,39].
Conducting-polymer hydrogels (PEDOT:PSS; PPy/PANI-based systems)
Low interfacial impedance and high electronic conductivity are achievable; optimized PEDOT:PSS hydrogels can also provide stretchability and wet stability.

Chronic behavior depends on hydration, dopant/network organization, oxidation, and interfacial adhesion. A four-month coating study found better chronic recording stability for PEDOT/CNT than PEDOT:PSS, showing that initial impedance alone is not predictive.
Solution processing and advanced fabrication, including 3D printing, are feasible for optimized systems. Standardized material or device cost is not reported [[40], [41], [42]].
Predominantly ionic conductive hydrogels
Hydrated ions carry charge through compliant water-rich networks, providing tissue-like mechanics and ionic coupling.
Ion exchange/redistribution, dehydration, and excessive swelling can change impedance over time; cytocompatibility remains formulation- and salt/additive-dependent.
Casting, molding, and injection are generally accessible, but water management, packaging, and storage are critical. Quantitative cost comparisons are lacking [43,44].
Mixed ionic-electronic architectures
Simultaneous ionic and electronic transport can reduce the charge-conversion mismatch between tissue and electronic hardware while retaining soft mechanics.

Ionic and electronic phases may age on different time scales; hydration and morphology changes can alter coupled transport and interface impedance. Safety depends on both phases and possible leachables.
Printing and multilayer integration are possible, but multicomponent control increases manufacturing complexity. No standardized cost comparison is available [40,41].
Permanent covalent networks
A permanent polymer skeleton provides dimensional stability and can suppress excessive swelling when crosslink density is appropriately designed.

Irreversible bond rupture is not intrinsically self-healing; without dissipative or anti-fatigue mechanisms, cyclic damage can accumulate. Safety depends on crosslinker chemistry and residual monomer removal.
Chemistry can be reproducible, but crosslink density must be tightly controlled because it affects modulus, swelling, and diffusion simultaneously. Cost is rarely quantified [32].
Dynamic or covalent-dynamic hybrid networks
Reversible bonds dissipate energy, permit stress relaxation, and can support self-recovery; hybrid networks can combine a stable skeleton with adaptive interactions.

Time-dependent bond exchange can introduce creep or hysteresis if insufficiently constrained. Formulation-specific ligand/ion safety and long-term leaching must be evaluated; hybrid design can improve dimensional stability.

Mild gelation and injectability can aid processing, but reaction kinetics and environmental sensitivity complicate process control and sterilization validation. Cost is process-dependent and rarely quantified [24,32].

tables.label: Table 8
tables.caption: Material-specific safety risks, present evidence boundaries, and minimum evaluation requirements for conductive-hydrogel neural interfaces.
rows: Risk source
Main concern and exposure route
Direct evidence in the reviewed studies
Evidence boundary
Minimum evaluation and follow-up requirements
Residual monomers and oligomers
Unreacted acrylamide, acrylic acid, methacrylate or NHS-bearing species may diffuse from the hydrated network and cause local cytotoxicity, neurotoxicity or sensitization.
Representative studies generally report final-gel viability or short-term histology, but do not provide batch-specific residual-monomer concentrations [[20], [21], [22], [23], [24]].
Indirect only: acceptable cell viability does not demonstrate chemical absence or a safe chronic exposure margin.

Measure conversion and targeted residues by HPLC/LC-MS/GC-MS; perform exhaustive extractables testing and toxicological risk assessment on final, sterilized and aged devices; include acute cell assays and chronic implantation endpoints matched to intended use [144,145].
Crosslinkers, initiators and catalysts
APS/TEMED, photoinitiators, aldehydes, coupling reagents and coordination ions may remain reactive or generate toxic by-products.
Direct evidence is formulation-specific and is usually limited to cytocompatibility or short animal observations; complete residual profiles are rarely reported.
Hypothesis requiring testing: network formation or washing is often assumed to remove these species, but this cannot be inferred without analytical recovery data.

Quantify parent compounds and reaction products; validate washing, sterilization and shelf-life effects; use polar and non-polar extracts, dose-response cytotoxicity, sensitization/irritation where relevant, and subchronic-to-chronic local histology [144,145].
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs)
Potential release of free or fragmented CNTs, macrophage uptake, oxidative stress, persistence and migration from the implant site.
PAACP was evaluated in a rat sciatic-nerve system [22]. CNT-PVA microelectrodes recorded for up to 8 months, but GFAP/Iba-1 histology mainly covered 3-30 days [85].
Direct device function is not equivalent to chronic filler safety; long-term release, biodistribution and clearance remain unquantified.

Characterize CNT loading, dispersion and bound/free fraction; quantify released material during cyclic ageing; assess neural and macrophage responses, local nerve conduction, quantitative histology and, where release is plausible, organ distribution at staged chronic endpoints including ≥ 6 months for permanent devices.
MXene
Oxidation, sheet fragmentation and release of Ti-containing or surface-termination species may alter ROS generation, immune response and electrical performance.
The MXene/PEDOT:PSS/TA-containing ICAA interface showed stable function and reduced tissue injury over 4 weeks in a rat vagus-nerve model [24].
Direct for that final formulation and 4-week model only; it does not establish chronic MXene biodistribution, clearance or class-wide safety.

Track oxidation state, particle size and soluble/particulate release during PBS/serum ageing; use ICP-MS and microscopy where appropriate; test ROS, neural/glial and macrophage responses, local histology and biodistribution over durations matched to a permanent implant.
PEDOT:PSS
PSS-rich fractions, low-molecular-weight additives, dedoping products or polymer fragments may leach; electrical overdrive may change local chemistry.
T-ECH, TN-H and ICAA provide formulation-specific cytocompatibility, electrochemical or short-term in vivo evidence [20,24,122]; several regeneration platforms also contain PEDOT:PSS [63,64,66].
Indirect for chronic neural safety: most studies do not combine long-term chemical release profiles with quantitative neural histology.

Measure extractables, TOC and targeted additives before and after sterilization/electrical cycling; monitor dedoping and degradation under worst-case stimulation; pair chemical data with neural viability, electrophysiology and quantitative 3-, 6- and 12-month histology when intended for permanent use.
Tannic acid (TA)
Dose-dependent protein binding, oxidation products and diffusible polyphenols may affect cells, coagulation or local redox balance.
TA is one component of ICAA, for which 4-week device-level compatibility was reported [24]; the biological contribution of TA was not isolated.
Indirect: safety of the composite cannot be assigned to TA alone, and a beneficial antioxidant assay does not substitute for release-dose characterization.

Quantify free TA and oxidation products during ageing; establish release-dose-response relationships in neural, glial and immune cells; assess hemocompatibility when blood exposure is plausible and include chronic local histology.
Nanoparticles and metal ions
BaTiO3, PDA nanoparticles and released Fe3+/Mg2+ or other ions may cause particle persistence, ion imbalance, ROS or off-target immune effects depending on dose and localization.

BaTiO3/collagen plus ultrasound directly altered astrocyte and Schwann-cell signaling in its tested repair models [67]; Fe3+- and Mg2+-containing regenerative systems provide separate, composition-specific evidence [54,61,62].
No class effect can be inferred across particle chemistry, dose, target tissue or stimulus. Mechanistic benefit does not itself demonstrate chronic systemic safety.

Measure particle size, dissolution and ion release by validated analytical methods; determine local dose, biodistribution and organ retention; test ROS, immune activation, genotoxicity where indicated, and quantitative local/systemic histology over the intended exposure period.
Degradation products
Acidic/basic fragments, oligomers, particles or ions may change pH, osmolality, inflammation and electrical/mechanical integrity as the network degrades.

Reviewed studies commonly report mass loss, swelling or retained function, whereas identities, concentrations and toxicity of intermediate products are seldom resolved [64,[93], [94], [95], [96], [97], [98], [99], [100], [101], [102], [103], [104]].
Mostly hypothetical until the actual product spectrum and clinically relevant exposure are measured; nominal biodegradability is not proof of harmless resorption.

Combine real-time and accelerated hydrolytic, oxidative and enzymatic ageing with LC-MS/GC-MS/SEC/ICP-MS as appropriate; test worst-case product mixtures at measured concentrations and align degradation, nerve regeneration and histology time courses.
Extractables and leachables
Additives, solvents, surfactants, adhesives, packaging constituents and sterilization-generated species may be released from the final assembled device.
A comprehensive final-device extractables/leachables profile is not reported for the representative neural-interface systems reviewed here.
Evidence gap: material-purity statements and single-component tests cannot substitute for final finished-device chemical characterization.

Apply ISO 10993-18-aligned exhaustive extraction using justified polar/non-polar media, analytical evaluation thresholds and targeted elemental analysis; identify and quantify constituents and perform ISO 10993-17 toxicological risk assessment on sterilized and aged devices [140,145].
Inflammation and histological observation duration
Acute injury can evolve into macrophage/microglial activation, astrogliosis, fibrosis, axonal loss, demyelination or compression neuropathy after early time points.

Model-specific evidence includes 4-week ICAA vagus-nerve histology [24], 8-week graphene-membrane sciatic-nerve inflammation [39], early 3-30-day GFAP/Iba-1 assessment for the 8-month CNT-PVA recording study [85], and long-term rabbit ECoG evidence in a different cortical platform [78].
Direct only for each stated material, anatomy, endpoint and duration. Cross-model comparison is indirect and cannot establish lifetime safety or absence of chronic compression.

Use blinded quantitative Iba-1/CD68, GFAP, fibrotic-capsule, NFM/S100/myelin and axon metrics with nerve conduction and device displacement/pressure where relevant; include acute, subchronic and ≥ 6-month endpoints for permanent implants, plus terminal organ histology when material release is plausible.
tables.footnotes: We have adopted a relatively conservative approach in labeling the evidence labels in Table 8. The direct evidence will not be used beyond the formula, anatomical site, end point and duration verified by it; Indirect analogy can only explain a certain possibility, and cannot be regarded as confirmatory evidence; As for the hypothesis, it cannot be presented as an established biological benefit. NR means not reported. The test plan should be designed according to the expected tissue contact type, implantation duration, degradation behavior, and the sterilization or aging state in the worst case, rather than all hydrogels follow the same process.
